results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 45 aligned units: the outliner's summary states the controlling idea of the spec paragraph it is aligned to, in the spec's order. The two opening callouts match no spec paragraph (they carry the thesis statement and roadmap by placement).
The outliner marked no unit as holding two ideas.
Every unit serves one of S1 to S6; the opening, usage and closing units serve S6 and the part's closing.

Each table is introduced by the sentence before it; Figures 1, 2 and 3 are read in the text of p24 and p34 and by their captions; each spec evidence item appears in its paragraph. The unexplained four-hour queue in the volumes table is recorded under flow_is_followable, where both flow readers raised it.

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary (for example 'Seen whole', 'All of those systems hold data about the same goods', 'These are the systems Noor did not choose', 'To answer these incidents', 'Because these facts are fixed'). Both flow readers found each section linked to the one before.

results.spec_locus: p24 (/sections landscape, evidence: stock chain intervals and 'up to two hours')
results.quote: The sentence before gives the hops as 15 minutes, one hour and one hour, and then the connector passing it on to the marketplaces. I added them and got two hours and a quarter or more, so I re-read to see what I had missed. I did not find out.
results.finding: Both flow readers stopped on the stock chain: the hops as listed add up to more than the 'up to two hours' the same paragraph states, and neither could resolve it. The draft repeats the figures the spec prescribes (and the ledger behind it; the spec's open questions already record this).

results.spec_locus: p19 evidence (volumes table, 'Delays at peak') and p39 evidence ('the four-hour WMS queue')
results.draft_locus: The Volumes Every Design Is Sized Against ¶1
results.quote: The four-hour order queue is never explained on this page; it returns once more in the Black Friday story as "the four-hour WMS queue" and that is all. I looked for the cause and did not find one.
results.finding: Both flow readers looked for the cause of the four-hour order queue and found none. The two-hour stock delay in the same table row is explained two sections later; the queue is stated twice (volumes table, p39) and no spec unit is given the job of explaining it.

results.spec_locus: p09 controlling idea and section growth controlling idea ('a dozen systems')
results.quote: "a dozen systems" in 2023 did not match my count from the table just above (I counted about nine by 2023; the data warehouse, returns portal and EDI come later), nor the "thirteen" of the key points.
results.finding: Both flow readers set 'a dozen systems to join' (2023) against the growth table and against the 'thirteen systems' of the key points and p22, and were left unsure whether these are the same count. The phrase is the spec's own (p09 and the section's controlling idea).

results.spec_locus: p30 (/sections waypoint, evidence: ownership in W1, W3, W7 before hubs in W1, W2, W3)
results.quote: the same decisions appear in both groups (W1 and W3 are named under owners and under hubs), the hubs are dated the same quarters as the ownership (Q3 and Q4 2027) ... So I could not see, from the table, what "first" and "then" separate. I took it to mean order of reasoning, not order of time, but the page does not say so.
results.finding: Both flow readers re-read this paragraph and went back to the table's 'When' column to find what 'first' and 'then' order; reader 1 re-read here most and did not settle it, reader 2 settled it after a short re-read. The prose does not say that the priority is one of reasoning and not of dates. The declared order of ideas is sound; the grouping of W1 and W3 under both owners and hubs comes from the spec's evidence, but one clause in the draft would remove the doubt.

results.quote: I re-read this. The three sizes are listed from this page backwards (third page, second, first), while the sentences that follow walk the same way but I first tried to map them onto pages one, two, three.
results.finding: Both flow readers had to re-read the first sentence of the conclusion: 'one company, the patterns many companies share, and every commerce platform' lists the three preface pages in reverse reading order without saying which page is which, so the reader maps the three sizes to the pages before the following sentences fall into place.

results.spec_locus: /thesis/claim and p02 ('warehouse stock is copied along a chain of four')
results.quote: "A chain of four" was not clear to me when I first met it: four systems, four copies or four hops? The systems section later lists five holders of the number (WMS, ERP, platform, connector, marketplaces) joined by four hops and calls it "four copies of one number" ... I went back to the opening to check which was meant.
results.finding: One flow reader could not tell what the 'four' in 'a chain of four' counts and went back to the opening from p24. The wording is the spec's (p02, thesis; see its open question on 'stock in four'). Reported by one reader only.

results.spec_locus: p27 (/sections problems, the ten incidents in the ledger's numbering)
results.draft_locus: The Problems Kestrel & Pine Starts 2027 With ¶1
results.quote: The incident list has no visible order of its own. It is not by date ... and not by kind, since the closing paragraph groups "incidents 1 to 7 and 9" with number 8 sitting in the middle. The lead-in says the numbers are the ones chapters cite, which tells me the order is fixed but not what it is. I stopped looking for a pattern after the fourth item.
results.finding: One flow reader looked for the principle that orders the ten incidents and found none; the lead sentence says the numbers are fixed but not what they follow. The order is the spec's and the ledger's (decision log: renumbering rejected). Reported by one reader only.

results.spec_locus: p41 and section examples controlling idea ('the four stories of 2027 test its priorities'); p37 evidence
results.quote: Bergzicht's reorder already has SSCC labels and a despatch advice sent at pack confirmation (which is W6 working), while Eva's order still travels by the iPaaS and stock "trickles back through the ERP" (the old way). So some stories show Waypoint in effect and some show the landscape before it, and I was not sure which each one was meant to be.
results.finding: One flow reader could not tell how the four 2027 stories 'test' Waypoint: the section says they fall before its hubs arrive, yet the stories do not say which of them show the old landscape and which show a Waypoint decision already at work. Whether the prose or the spec's account of the stories has to say this is not decidable from the inputs. Reported by one reader only.

results.spec_locus: /intent/audience/does_not_know (OMS); thesis statement placement: KEY POINTS callout
results.quote: adds an availability service (which computes what each channel may still sell), an order management system and a product information system beside the existing platform
results.finding: 'Order management system' is used in the third key point with no gloss, although system of record, availability service and replatforming are each glossed in the same sentence; it is explained only at p22 ('would coordinate orders from every channel, with shared payment, fulfillment, delivery and return states').

results.spec_locus: /intent/audience/does_not_know (PIM); thesis statement placement: KEY POINTS callout
results.quote: an order management system and a product information system beside the existing platform
results.finding: 'Product information system' is used in the third key point with no gloss; it is explained only at p12 ('one place where product content and attributes are kept and published to every channel').

results.spec_locus: /intent/audience/already_knows (a commerce platform is the whole set of systems); p02
results.quote: keeping the hosted commerce platform it already has
results.finding: The reader arrives with the book's wide sense of 'commerce platform' (the whole set of systems that make and keep promises). The opening uses 'the platform' and 'the hosted commerce platform' for one product before the 2016 row of the growth table says what that product is, and the page never says it is using the word in the narrower sense, so 'keeps the platform' can be read against the wrong meaning.

results.draft_locus: The Problems Kestrel & Pine Starts 2027 With ¶1
results.quote: €2,900 in PSP fees for declined authorizations
results.finding: 'Authorizations' is never explained on the page; the incident's cost figure depends on knowing that an authorization is a request to approve a card payment and that a declined one still costs a fee.

results.quote: a refund of **€199** by iDEAL reversal, booked as a credit note
results.finding: 'Credit note' is never explained on the page.

results.draft_locus: The Problems Kestrel & Pine Starts 2027 With ¶1
results.quote: about **€8,200** of margin lost, and a price-parity warning from a marketplace
results.finding: 'Price-parity warning' is never explained; the reader has to work out that a marketplace forbids a lower price elsewhere.

results.spec_locus: p07 (first use); also p18, p22, W1, p38
results.quote: need different prices, payment terms and fulfillment
results.finding: 'Fulfillment' (and 'fulfilled', 'seller-fulfilled', 'fulfillment program') is a core commerce term used six or more times and never explained in a clause.
The opening picks up the previous page, states a disputable claim and gives a roadmap; none of the weak patterns.
The closing synthesizes the three preface pages, calls back to the book's opening numbers and hands off to Part I; no new subtopic, no body evidence, not a rephrased thesis only.

p43 gives the spec's synthesis (incidents as instances of the patterns, patterns as promises broken at the joins, Waypoint's priority as the book's claim in one company's program) and p44 the course-of-action takeaway. The so-what is carried by 'you can now name the systems behind each' and the question to ask at each handoff; the spec's 'check any figure against this page' is said in the preceding section and the opening, not in the last section, and no conclusion paragraph in the spec is assigned it.
'The book opened on two numbers, order #1072455 and 1,340 oversold units. They have returned here as the recurring order and as incident 1.'

The intro reader predicted the business (glance, growth, catalog, channels, volumes), the people and systems, the ten incidents, Waypoint, the five recurring examples and the usage section, in that order, with invented but consistent figures in tables and no outside sources.

The reader gave the chain (WMS to ERP every 15 minutes, hourly to the platform, hourly to the connector), the sell-out at 19:40, up to two hours, 1,340 units, and 'the platform is not what failed; the joins failed' with W4.
The reader gave order #1052877 with its three statuses for six days, Schrödinger's Order, and W2 as a bought OMS that becomes the one order record for every channel.

The reader gave the eight as one fact in several systems with no agreed owner and no reliable way for copies to learn of a change, and the other two (Card-Testing Night, Deprecated Endpoint) as what the outside world does to a landscape nobody watches as a whole. The reader also noted that 'each is an instance of a pattern named on the previous page' does not hold for incident 8, which the list calls 'a trust failure rather than one of the sixteen patterns'.
The rubric reader found no disagreeing pair against the ledger or between tables; 27.0 + 12.0 + 6.0 + 3.0 = 48.0. Facts on the page that the ledger does not state are not disagreements.

Fictional in both callouts, in the lead and in the Sources line; every Kestrel & Pine system is named by role; marketplaces and carriers are said to be real with invented dealings. The reader noted that the payment brands are not covered by that sentence and that the carrier PostNL sits in Figure 3's list of 'seven systems'; neither names the vendor of a Kestrel & Pine system.
The reader named returns-and-exchanges and commerce-payments, and The Boomerang and The Message in a Bottle.
The reader named Noor Visser, Head of Engineering since January 2027: new to this company, not new to engineering, asked to decide about systems she did not choose.
